qns_content.text: A system at constant volume absorbs 208 J of heat, and its temperature increases from 300 K to 310 K. What is \( C_v \)? (1 mol diatomic gas)

text_solutions: For a diatomic ideal gas at constant volume, \( \Delta U = q_v = nC_v\Delta T \). Given \( q_v = 208 \, \text{J} \), \( n = 1 \, \text{mol} \), \( \Delta T = 310 - 300 = 10 \, \text{K} \), we get \( 208 = 1 \times C_v \times 10 \), so \( C_v = 208 / 10 = 20.8 \, \text{J/mol·K} \), typical for a diatomic gas (\( C_v \approx 2.5R \)).

text_solutions: The standard enthalpy change for a reaction forming a compound from its elements in their standard states is the enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\circ\)) multiplied by the moles formed. For \(2NH_3\), \(\Delta H = 2 \times \Delta_f H^\circ (NH_3)\).

Which thermodynamic quantity is a measure of disorder in a system?

text_solutions: Entropy (\(S\)) is a measure of the disorder or randomness in a system, as defined in thermodynamics.

text_solutions: For an exothermic reaction at constant pressure, heat evolved \(q_p = \Delta H\), and since it’s exothermic, \(\Delta H < 0\), so \(q_p = \Delta H\).

text_solutions: For an ideal gas in an isothermal process (\(\Delta T = 0\)), \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = 0\), regardless of the path.

text_solutions: For an ideal gas, \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T\). In an isothermal process (\(\Delta T = 0\)), \(\Delta U = 0\).

text_solutions: At constant pressure, \(\Delta H = q_p\). Here, \(q = 1200 \, \text{J}\) (heat absorbed), so \(\Delta H = 1200 \, \text{J}\).

What is the change in internal energy (\( \Delta U \)) for the vaporization of 1 mol of water at 373 K if \( \Delta H = 40.79 \, \text{kJ/mol} \)? (\( R = 8.314 \, \text{J/mol·K} \))

text_solutions: For \( \ce{H2O(l) \rightarrow H2O(g)} \), \( \Delta n_g = 1 \). Using \( \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT \), where \( RT = 8.314 \times 373 \times 10^{-3} = 3.1012 \, \text{kJ} \), we get \( \Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT = 40.79 - 3.1012 = 37.69 \, \text{kJ/mol} \).

text_solutions: For \( \ce{H2O(l) \rightarrow H2O(g)} \) at 373 K, \( \Delta S_{sys} = \frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T} = \frac{40.79 \times 10^3}{373} = 109.4 \, \text{J/K} \), representing the entropy increase due to phase change from liquid to gas.

qns_content.text: In a process, 300 J of heat is absorbed by a system, and 100 J of work is done on the system. What is \(\Delta U\)?

text_solutions: Using the first law: \(\Delta U = q + w\). Here, \(q = +300 \, \text{J}\) (heat absorbed), \(w = +100 \, \text{J}\) (work done on system), so \(\Delta U = 300 + 100 = 400 \, \text{J}\).

A system absorbs 500 J of heat and performs 200 J of work. What is the change in internal energy (\(\Delta U\))?

text_solutions: Using the first law: \(\Delta U = q + w\). Here, \(q = +500 \, \text{J}\) (heat absorbed), \(w = -200 \, \text{J}\) (work done by system), so \(\Delta U = 500 - 200 = 300 \, \text{J}\).

qns_content.text: A reaction has \(\Delta H = -100 \, \text{kJ}\) and \(\Delta S = -200 \, \text{J/K}\). At what temperature does it become spontaneous?
A reaction has \( \Delta H = 80.00 \, \text{kJ/mol} \), \( \Delta S = 200.0 \, \text{J/K·mol} \), and is spontaneous at 450 K. What is \( \Delta G \) at 450 K?

text_solutions: \( \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = 80.00 - 450 \times 0.2000 = 80.00 - 90.00 = -10.00 \, \text{kJ/mol} \). The negative \( \Delta G \) confirms the reaction is spontaneous at 450 K.

text_solutions: For a spontaneous process at constant \(T\) and \(P\), the Gibbs free energy must decrease (\(\Delta G < 0\)), as it determines spontaneity under these conditions.

text_solutions: Moles of \( CO_2 = 22 / 44 = 0.5 \, \text{mol} \). For \( C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) \), \( \Delta H = -393.5 \, \text{kJ/mol} \). Heat released = \( 0.5 \times 393.5 = 196.75 \, \text{kJ} \) (positive, as heat is released in exothermic reaction).

qns_content.text: For an isolated system with \(\Delta U = 0\), what can be said about \(\Delta S\)?

text_solutions: For an isolated system, a spontaneous process increases entropy (\(\Delta S > 0\)) until equilibrium, where \(\Delta S = 0\). Since \(\Delta U = 0\), \(\Delta S > 0\) for spontaneity.

text_solutions: The standard state of an element is its most stable form at 1 bar and 298 K. For carbon, this is graphite.

qns_content.text: For the reaction \( 2A(g) \rightarrow B(g) \), \( \Delta H = -40.00 \, \text{kJ/mol} \), \( \Delta S = -100.0 \, \text{J/K·mol} \) at 300 K. What is \( \Delta G \)?

text_solutions: \( \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -40.00 - 300 \times (-0.1000) = -40.00 + 30.00 = -10.00 \, \text{kJ/mol} \). The negative \( \Delta G \) indicates spontaneity at 300 K.

For the reaction \(2Cl(g) \rightarrow Cl_2(g)\), what are the signs of \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\)?

text_solutions: Bond formation is exothermic (\(\Delta H < 0\)), and entropy decreases as two particles form one (\(\Delta S < 0\)).

qns_content.text: The enthalpy of neutralization of a strong acid with a strong base is approximately:

qns_content.text: Calculate \( \Delta S_{sys} \) for the condensation of 1 mol of ethanol at 351 K. (\( \Delta H_{vap} = 38.6 \, \text{kJ/mol} \))

text_solutions: For \( C_2H_5OH(g) \rightarrow C_2H_5OH(l) \), \( \Delta S_{sys} = -\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{T} = -\frac{38.6 \times 10^3}{351} \approx -110.0 \, \text{J/K·mol} \), as condensation decreases entropy.

text_solutions: Entropy decreases when disorder decreases, e.g., \(H_2O(l) \rightarrow H_2O(s)\), as liquid to solid reduces randomness.

text_solutions: Reverse second: \(\Delta H = 283 \, \text{kJ}\). Add third: \(\Delta H = 241.8 \, \text{kJ}\). Subtract first: \(\Delta H = 283 + 241.8 - 393.5 = 131.3 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

qns_content.text: A reaction has \(\Delta H = 60 \, \text{kJ/mol}\) and \(\Delta S = 150 \, \text{J/K}\). At what temperature does \(\Delta G = 0\)?

text_solutions: For an endothermic process (\(\Delta H > 0\)) with \(\Delta S > 0\), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\). It becomes spontaneous (\(\Delta G < 0\)) at high temperatures when \(T\Delta S > \Delta H\).

qns_content.text: Calculate \( \Delta S_{sys} \) for the vaporization of 36 g of ethanol at 351 K if \( \Delta H_{vap} = 38.6 \, \text{kJ/mol} \). (Molar mass of \( C_2H_5OH = 46.07 \, \text{g/mol} \))

text_solutions: Moles = \( 36 / 46.07 \approx 0.7812 \, \text{mol} \). For vaporization, \( \Delta S_{sys} = n \times \Delta H_{vap} / T = 0.7812 \times 38.6 \times 10^3 / 351 \approx 86.0 \, \text{J/K} \).

qns_content.text: Which of the following is true for an endothermic process where \(\Delta S < 0\)?

text_solutions: For an endothermic process, \(\Delta H > 0\). If \(\Delta S < 0\), then \(T\Delta S < 0\), and \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S > 0\), making the process non-spontaneous at all temperatures.

text_solutions: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\). When \(\Delta n_g = 0\) (no change in moles of gas), \(\Delta H = \Delta U\), as in \(H_2(g) + Cl_2(g) \rightarrow 2HCl(g)\).

text_solutions: \( \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S = -80.00 - 300 \times (-0.2000) = -80.00 + 60.00 = -20.00 \, \text{kJ/mol} \). The negative \( \Delta G \) indicates spontaneity at 300 K.

Which of the following statements is true for a reversible adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas?

text_solutions: In a reversible adiabatic process (\(q = 0\)), \(\Delta U = w\). For an ideal gas, \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T\), and since expansion cools the gas, \(\Delta T < 0\), making \(\Delta U < 0\).

qns_content.text: For an ideal gas (\( \gamma = 1.67 \)) compressed adiabatically from \(V_1 = 12\,\text{L}\) to \(V_2 = 3\,\text{L}\), starting at \(T_1 = 300\,\text{K}\), calculate the work done on the gas if \( C_v = 12.47 \, \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \). (Assume \(n=1\) mol.)

text_solutions:
For an adiabatic ideal-gas process, \( T_2 = T_1 (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma-1} = 300 \times 4^{0.67} \approx 300 \times 2.5315 = 759.45 \,\text{K} \).

With \( q=0 \), \( w = \Delta U = n C_v (T_2 - T_1) = 1 \times 12.47 \times (759.45 - 300) \approx 5729 \,\text{J} \).

Since the work is done on the gas, it is positive: \( w \approx +5729 \,\text{J} \).

text_solutions: For reactions at constant temperature (ideal gas), \( \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT \). With \( \Delta n_g = 0 \), \( \Delta H = \Delta U = 250 \,\text{J} \).

qns_content.text: For the reaction \(N_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightarrow 2NO(g)\), \(\Delta H = 180.6 \, \text{kJ/mol}\) at 298 K. What is \(\Delta U\) if the gas behaves ideally? (\(R = 8.314 \, \text{J/mol·K}\))

text_solutions: \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 2 = 0\), \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\). Since \(\Delta n_g = 0\), \(\Delta U = \Delta H = 180.6 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

qns_content.text: For the reaction \(H_2(g) + I_2(g) \rightarrow 2HI(g)\), \(\Delta H = 52.96 \, \text{kJ/mol}\) at 298 K. What is \(\Delta U\)? (\(R = 8.314 \, \text{J/mol·K}\))

text_solutions: \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 2 = 0\), so \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT = \Delta U\). Thus, \(\Delta U = 52.96 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

In an isobaric process, 600 J of heat is supplied, and the system does 200 J of work. What is \(\Delta U\)?

text_solutions: At constant pressure, \(\Delta H = q_p = 600 \, \text{J}\), \(w = -200 \, \text{J}\) (work done by system). \(\Delta U = q + w = 600 - 200 = 400 \, \text{J}\).

qns_content.text: Calculate \(\Delta G^\circ\) for a reaction with \(K = 10^4\) at 298 K. (\(R = 8.314 \, \text{J/mol·K}\))
For a reversible isothermal compression of an ideal gas, the heat absorbed is:

text_solutions: For an isothermal process (\(\Delta U = 0\)), \(\Delta U = q + w = 0\), so \(q = -w\). For reversible compression, \(w = -nRT \ln(V_2/V_1)\) (positive), so \(q = nRT \ln(V_2/V_1)\), which is negative since \(V_2 < V_1\).

text_solutions: In an isochoric process (\(\Delta V = 0\)), work done \(w = -P\Delta V = 0\), regardless of other conditions.

qns_content.text: A system absorbs 600 J of heat at constant volume, and its internal energy increases by 600 J. What is the work done?

text_solutions: At constant volume, \(w = -P\Delta V = 0\). First Law: \(\Delta U = q + w = 600 + 0 = 600 \, \text{J}\), so \(w = 0 \, \text{J}\).

qns_content.text: For a reaction at constant volume, the heat absorbed is equal to:

text_solutions: At constant volume, \(w = -p\Delta V = 0\), so from the first law, \(\Delta U = q_v\), the heat absorbed at constant volume.

text_solutions: The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, i.e., \(C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)\).

text_solutions: At constant volume, \(\Delta U = q_v = nC_v\Delta T\). So, \(800 = n \times 20 \times 10\), \(n = 800 / 200 = 4 \, \text{mol}\).

qns_content.text: For the vaporization of 72 g of water at 373 K (\( \Delta H_{vap} = 40.79 \, \text{kJ/mol} \), molar mass = 18 g/mol), what is \( \Delta S_{sys} \)?

text_solutions: Moles = \( 72 / 18 = 4 \, \text{mol} \). For vaporization, \( \Delta S_{sys} = n \times \Delta H_{vap} / T = 4 \times 40790 / 373 \approx 437.48 \, \text{J/K} \approx 437.5 \, \text{J/K} \).
